name: Multiplayer Game Backend
description: Design a multiplayer game backend handling real-time state synchronization, matchmaking, and session management. Covers authoritative game servers, low-latency state caching, and asynchronous matchmaking workers.

learnSteps.title: Real-Time State via WebSocket
learnSteps.description: Game clients maintain persistent WebSocket connections through the Load Balancer to authoritative Game Servers. The LB uses least-connections routing to ensure even distribution. Each Game Server hosts multiple game sessions, running a tick-based loop (e.g., 60 Hz) that processes player inputs, updates game state, and broadcasts state deltas back to all connected clients in the session.

learnSteps.title: In-Memory Game State with Redis
learnSteps.description: The authoritative game state for each active session lives in Redis, enabling sub-millisecond reads/writes. Redis Sorted Sets track leaderboards, and Hash types store player positions and inventories. When a Game Server crashes, another can resume the session by loading state from Redis. The TTL ensures abandoned sessions are garbage-collected automatically.

learnSteps.title: Asynchronous Matchmaking
learnSteps.description: When a player queues for a match, the Game Server publishes a matchmaking request to Kafka. Matchmaking Workers consume these requests and run ELO/MMR-based algorithms to form balanced teams. Once a match is formed, the worker writes the match assignment to PostgreSQL and notifies the Game Server, which then routes players to the allocated session.

learnSteps.title: Persistence and Player Profiles
learnSteps.description: Player profiles, match history, inventories, and progression are durably stored in PostgreSQL. Game Servers write match results and reward grants at session end. Read replicas serve profile lookups and leaderboard queries. The separation of hot state (Redis) from cold state (PostgreSQL) lets the system handle millions of concurrent players while keeping match data durable.

chaosScenarios.name: Game Server Instance Crash
chaosScenarios.description: Kill one of the 50 game server instances while it hosts live sessions
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: ~2% of active sessions lose their authoritative server. Affected clients disconnect and trigger a reconnect surge through the LB. A replacement server loads session state from Redis; players see a 5-10s freeze and roll back to the last persisted tick.
mitigationSteps: LB health check ejects the dead instance within 5s (5000ms interval)
Session orchestrator reassigns orphaned sessions to a healthy server, which restores state from Redis
Clients reconnect with jittered exponential backoff to avoid stampeding the LB
Capture core dump before terminating the instance; check for tick-loop deadlock

chaosScenarios.name: Game State Cache Latency Spike
chaosScenarios.description: Inject 50ms latency on Redis state operations (simulates BGSAVE fork stall or replica sync pressure)
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: State reads/writes that normally take <1ms blow the 16ms tick budget at 60Hz. Servers skip ticks, players see rubber-banding, and per-session input queues back up. Sessions stay alive but playability degrades platform-wide.
mitigationSteps: Game servers fall back to in-process state with write-behind flushes to Redis
Move RDB snapshots to a replica; keep AOF fsync at everysec, never always
Shed cosmetic sync (leaderboards) before gameplay-critical state
Fail over to the Redis replica if degradation persists beyond 5 minutes

chaosScenarios.name: Matchmaking Pipeline Stall
chaosScenarios.description: Partition the matchmaking Kafka topic from its consumer group, stalling match formation
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: In-progress matches are unaffected. New match requests accumulate in Kafka; queue times grow from seconds to minutes. Consumer-lag alarms fire and player cancel/requeue churn rises after ~2 minutes of waiting.
mitigationSteps: Check consumer-group lag and partition assignment; restart crash-looping workers
Widen MMR matching bands progressively to drain the backlog faster
Surface queue-time estimates to clients to reduce cancel/requeue churn
Replay unprocessed match requests after the partition heals (24h retention covers it)

bottleneckProgression.description: Tick loops saturate the 8-core instances; combat-heavy sessions exceed the 16ms frame budget at 60Hz
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Scale the fleet out, apply interest management (sync only entities near each player), and drop tick rate for low-activity sessions

bottleneckProgression.description: State delta read/write fan-out saturates Redis network throughput; replication lag grows
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Shard the state cluster by session ID, compress deltas, and pin hot sessions to dedicated shards

bottleneckProgression.description: Persistent WebSocket connection tables exhaust LB capacity at roughly two connections per active player
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Add LB instances behind DNS/anycast and shard players by region

expectedIssues.title: Tick Budget Overrun
expectedIssues.description: The 16ms processing time per tick leaves zero headroom at 60Hz; GC pauses or a single hot session cause skipped ticks and visible rubber-banding
expectedIssues.mitigation: Pre-allocate object pools to avoid GC, budget 10ms per tick with alerting at 13ms, and isolate heavyweight sessions onto dedicated instances

expectedIssues.title: Reconnect Storm After Network Blip
expectedIssues.description: A transient LB or ISP blip disconnects tens of thousands of WebSockets that all reconnect simultaneously, spiking auth and state-restore load
expectedIssues.mitigation: Client-side jittered backoff, reconnect tokens that skip full re-auth, and connection-rate limiting at the LB

expectedIssues.title: Match-End Write Bursts
expectedIssues.description: Synchronized session ends (mode rotations, timed events) flush thousands of match results at once, saturating the 500-connection PostgreSQL pool
expectedIssues.mitigation: Stagger result writes with jitter, buffer them through the queue, and front the database with a connection pooler

expectedIssues.title: Hot Session Concentration
expectedIssues.description: A single authoritative session cannot be split across servers; tournament or streamer lobbies with heavy spectator counts overload one instance
expectedIssues.mitigation: Move spectator fan-out onto a broadcast tier that reads state from Redis instead of the session-owning server

expectedIssues.title: Matchmaking Starvation at Distribution Tails
expectedIssues.description: Very high/low MMR players and off-peak regions wait far beyond the p95 target because candidate pools are thin
expectedIssues.mitigation: Time-based MMR band widening and cross-region matching fallback with hard latency caps

steps: Drain new session allocation away from the failing instance group
Verify orphaned sessions resumed from Redis; manually requeue any stuck sessions
Roll back the latest server build if the crash signature matches a recent deploy
Capture core dumps before terminating instances
Check Kafka consumer-group lag and partition assignment
Restart stuck workers and verify offsets advance
Temporarily widen MMR bands to drain the backlog
Announce queue delays in-game if waits exceed 5 minutes
Determine whether latency stems from BGSAVE/AOF activity or network saturation
Fail over to the replica if the primary is degraded

Audit sessions for state rollback after recovery

decisions.title: Authoritative Server Model
decisions.context: Multiplayer games must prevent client-side cheating and resolve conflicting player inputs deterministically
decisions.decision: All game state mutations run in server-side tick loops; clients send inputs and receive state deltas over WebSocket
consequences: Cheating via client tampering is structurally limited
Server fleet cost scales with concurrent sessions
Client-side prediction is required to hide the 30ms+ network RTT

decisions.title: Hot/Cold State Split (Redis vs PostgreSQL)
decisions.context: Tick loops need sub-millisecond state access, but match results and progression must be durable
decisions.decision: Active session state lives in Redis with TTL-based garbage collection; results and profiles persist to PostgreSQL at session end
consequences: Sub-ms reads keep the 16ms tick budget intact
A crash between persistence points can lose a few seconds of unflushed state
Session resume after a server failure is possible by reloading from Redis

decisions.title: Asynchronous Matchmaking via Kafka
decisions.context: Matchmaking tolerates seconds of latency, unlike gameplay; login rushes create extreme demand spikes
decisions.decision: Game servers publish match requests to Kafka; a separately scaled worker pool runs MMR-based matching
consequences: The queue absorbs login-rush spikes without affecting live sessions
Matchmaking capacity scales independently of the game server fleet
Adds seconds of queueing latency, acceptable for this workflow

tradeoffs.benefit: State operations stay in-memory and tick loops never block on disk
tradeoffs.cost: A server crash can roll players back several seconds of gameplay

tradeoffs.benefit: A single trusted source of truth for game state
tradeoffs.cost: 50+ instances at peak versus near-zero server cost for peer-to-peer

tradeoffs.benefit: MMR bands widen over time so players always get a match
tradeoffs.cost: Off-peak and tail-MMR matches are less balanced

alternatives.name: Peer-to-Peer Lockstep
alternatives.description: Clients exchange inputs directly and simulate the game deterministically
alternatives.prosVsCons: Near-zero server cost and minimal peer latency, but trivially cheatable, fragile under NAT and packet loss, and desyncs are hard to recover
alternatives.whyNotChosen: Competitive integrity and reconnect support require an authoritative source of truth

alternatives.name: In-Process State Only (No Redis)
alternatives.description: Keep session state purely in game-server memory
alternatives.prosVsCons: Removes a network hop per tick, but a server crash permanently kills every session it hosts
alternatives.whyNotChosen: Session resume from Redis was judged worth the ~1ms overhead per state operation

alternatives.name: Synchronous Matchmaking RPC
alternatives.description: Game servers call a matchmaking service directly and wait for assignment
alternatives.prosVsCons: Simpler to reason about, but couples login-rush spikes to gameplay capacity and retries amplify load
alternatives.whyNotChosen: Queue-based decoupling isolates matchmaking surges from live sessions
